Reconstructed records should therefore be assessed field by field and not treated as completely interchangeable with native ones.
item.dc:creator: Nikita A. Klimin (HSE University, Moscow, Russia)

item.title: Tiny Suffix Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2610.35543v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Suffix array and inverse suffix array queries on a text of length $n$ can be answered in $\widetilde{O}(\tau^3)$ time using an auxiliary data structure occupying $O(n/\tau)$ words, for any $\tau \in [1,n]$.
item.dc:creator: Sharma V. Thankachan

item.title: Navigating Ideation Space: Decomposed Conceptual Representations for Positioning Scientific Ideas
item.description: arXiv:2601.08901v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific discovery requires new ideas to be situated within an ever-expanding landscape of existing knowledge. An emerging challenge is how to identify conceptually relevant prior work from rapidly growing literature, and assess how a new idea differentiates from existing research. Current embedding approaches typically conflate distinct conceptual aspects into single representations and cannot support fine-grained retrieval; meanwhile, LLM-based evaluators are subject to sycophancy biases, failing to provide discriminative novelty assessment. We introduce the Ideation Space, a structured representation that decomposes scientific knowledge into three distinct dimensions learned through contrastive training. Our framework enables principled measurement of conceptual distance between ideas and modeling of ideation transitions that capture the logical connections within an idea. Building upon this representation, we propose a Hierarchical Sub-Space Retrieval framework for efficient, targeted literature retrieval, and a Decomposed Novelty Assessment algorithm that identifies which aspects of an idea are novel. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements, achieving Recall@30 of 0.329 (16.7% over the strongest baseline), and novelty assessment achieves promising correlation with expert judgments, outperforming all open-source LLM baselines up to 70B.
item.dc:creator: Minqian Liu, Yuexi Shen, Dawei Zhou, Lifu Huang

item.title: AllSERP: Exhaustive Per-Element Enrichment of the Versatile AdSERP Dataset
item.description: arXiv:2605.04949v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AdSERP is a public corpus of 2,776 search trials with eye gaze, cursor, scroll, pupil and click telemetry recorded on real Google result pages, together with the page screenshots and captured HTML. Its shipped bounding boxes cover only advertisements, which receive about 16 % of main-axis clicks. AllSERP adds a typed area-of-interest (AOI) layer for everything else: screenshot-anchored boxes for organic results, People-Also-Ask, image packs, local packs and other widgets, labelled from the captured HTML. Three typed flavours trade box tightness for coverage, from tight boxes to gap-filled boxes to per-card cells inside the top-ads carousel. The ad partition agrees with the shipped ad rectangles on all 38,250 comparisons, and box fidelity is measured on the full corpus with a DOM-based harness. Under the gap-filled flavour, 95.7 % of final clicks land in a typed main-axis AOI once cursor coordinates are converted into screenshot space. In a per-element inventory of clicks, fixations, regressions and above-fold exposure, attention and clicks dissociate by element type: 99.7 % of top-ads carousels are fixated but only 10 % of clicks land on them, and 44 % of People-Also-Ask boxes are fixated but only two clicks in the corpus land on one. We release the pipeline, per-trial JSON, corpus CSVs and a browser-based replay viewer.
item.dc:creator: K. Andrew Edmonds

item.title: An Interpretable CF-RL-TOPSIS Fusion Model for Skills-Aware Talent Recommendation
item.description: arXiv:2605.24155v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Effective skills-aware talent recommendation must balance behavioral transition patterns, trajectory-sensitive adaptation, and inspectable occupation-level criteria. Evidence from public benchmarks on how these signals interact, however, remains limited. This study proposes CF-RL-TOPSIS, an interpretable late-fusion model that integrates a transition-aware collaborative branch, a compact reinforcement-style occupation-family bandit, and an entropy-weighted TOPSIS branch constructed from six semantic proxies; the validation-selected fusion coefficients remain auditable. The model is evaluated on two frozen public ICT talent-history benchmarks, JobHop and Karrierewege, using repeated chronological top-5 ranking and paired Wilcoxon tests. On JobHop the full hybrid attains NDCG@5 = 0.3040 +/- 0.0073 and significantly surpasses repeat-last, item Markov, transition-aware collaborative filtering, the CF+TOPSIS hybrid, GRU4Rec, and SASRec (p <= 0.0039 across planned comparisons). On Karrierewege the hybrid remains competitive but does not significantly exceed the strongest Markov baseline, revealing a persistence-dominated setting in which the bandit branch appropriately shrinks to near-zero weight. Proxy-sensitivity, family-level deep Q-network, and runtime checks support this interpretation, and a worked user-level case shows how branch scores, criterion weights, and rank shifts can be inspected for an individual recommendation. The contribution is not a benchmark-agnostic superiority claim, but a reproducible account of the conditions under which transparent late fusion adds value beyond simple continuation heuristics. In semantically rich, non-saturating talent-history regimes the three branches reinforce one another; in persistence-dominated regimes the same architecture remains competitive through its collaborative backbone, with the adaptive branch correctly inactive.
item.dc:creator: \"Ozkan Canay

item.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Context Rot in Long-horizon Search
item.description: arXiv:2606.29718v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Extensive context has become the norm as Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in long-horizon search tasks. The concern that increasing context length degrades model capabilities, known as context rot, has become a widely recognized issue for these applications. However, in deep search scenarios, it remains unclear how models actually fail under extensive context, and to what extent existing methods can mitigate such failures. Through a systematic study of four flagship models across three benchmarks, we identify a previously overlooked phenomenon: under extensive context, models give up or provide uncertain incorrect answers long before exhausting the context window. We refer to these two failure modes as inconclusive search failures. We show that these are common failure modes even for easy and moderately difficult queries, suggesting premature termination on queries that the model is capable of solving. Based on these findings, we revisit methods to mitigate context rot, including context management and parallel sampling. For context management, we analyze seven methods across three categories and show that they are inherently test-time scaling strategies that redirect models from inconclusive search failures toward further exploration by decreasing the peak context length. We also provide model-dependent principles for method selection. For parallel sampling, we develop a behavior-aware filtering strategy and observe a performance gain of 2.6% to 4.9% across three aggregation methods.
item.dc:creator: Shijie Xia, Yikun Wang, Zhen Huang, Pengfei Liu

item.title: UniRec: Cross-stage Multi-Task Fusion with Preference Optimization for Cascaded Recommender Systems
item.description: arXiv:2609.11052v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Industrial recommender systems use cascaded stages with different candidate spaces, data distributions, and latency constraints. Each stage include multi-objective prediction and multi-task fusion (MTF) modules. Existing MTF methods typically design and optimize the fusion module independently for each stage, which can lead to inconsistent preferences across stages. Although cross-stage coordination methods have been proposed, they mainly transfer supervision to upstream scoring models rather than jointly optimizing the fusion modules. We propose UniRec, a Unified Cross-stage Recommendation Fusion framework that jointly optimizes pre-ranking and ranking fusion agents. UniRec employs a coupled dual-agent architecture with partially shared embeddings and stage-specific fusion functions. It further introduces Dual-Axis Preference Optimization to combine stage-local preferences with downstream-to-upstream preference transfer. To enable stable and efficient cross-stage training, we address two practical challenges: reward-induced distribution drift and the computational cost of pairwise preference learning. Extensive offline and online experiments on a production short-video system demonstrate consistent gains over single-stage fusion and cross-stage coordination baselines. In a nine-week online A/B test, UniRec improves total watch time by $0.675\%$ and app usage time by $0.616\%$, and active users by $0.189\%$, and has been fully deployed in production.
item.dc:creator: Lingyuan Kong, Jiaqi Cui, Fanjiao Zeng, Congqi Wang, Yu Li, Yuan Cheng, Jingxin Liu, Xiaoshuang Chen, Kaiqiao Zhan

item.title: Geometric Gain Graph: Zero-Token Graph Construction for Multi-Hop RAG
item.description: arXiv:2609.19622v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems struggle with multi-hop reasoning due to a fundamental inability to balance relevance and novelty. Traditional dense retrievers are constrained by surface-level matching, falling into a homogenized "Similarity Trap". Conversely, emerging Graph RAGs attempt to explore novel documents via heuristic entity extraction, but they introduce prohibitive Large Language Model (LLM) overhead and easily drift into off-topic "Novelty Traps". To fundamentally resolve this contradiction, we propose Geometric Gain Graph (G$^3$RAG), the novel zero-token graph construction paradigm for RAG. G$^3$RAG completely discards the expensive heuristic extraction by LLMs, aiming instead to directly quantify the information gain between nodes through the native document feature space. To this end, we designed a concise edge weight criterion, $\cos\theta \cdot \sin\theta$, which naturally maps the trade-off between relevance and novelty into a geometric measurement of directional consistency and orthogonality in the vector space, thereby driving the token-free topological construction of the graph. Furthermore, we introduce a topological penalty to suppress the excessive connectivity of high-frequency hubs, forcing the transient diffusion process toward long-tail peripheral nodes that carry critical indirect evidence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, while entirely eliminating LLM token costs during graph construction, G$^3$RAG significantly outperforms state-of-the-art Graph RAG baselines on complex multi-hop QA benchmarks. The code is available at: https://github.com/deeplearning-LI/G3RAG
item.dc:creator: Zeliang Li, Xiaofen Xing, Kailing Guo, Wenyu Tao, Xiangmin Xu

item.title: SearchJev: A Calibrated System-1 Model for Search Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.05107v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Search agents repeatedly make short decisions about relevance, evidence sufficiency, and search actions. Using generative language models for these decisions introduces latency and unreliable confidence. We present SearchJev, a calibrated System-1 model that separates search decisions from System-2 reasoning and generation. Given a search state and a decision schema, SearchJev scores legal options without autoregressive output generation. We propose Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions (SLCD) to learn decision probabilities from uncertain supervision and improve the reliability of decision confidence. In a dual-system search agent, SearchJev handles short decisions and delegates uncertain judgments to System 2, which retains planning, query generation, and answer composition. We also introduce SearchDecision-Bench, a benchmark unifying six types of search decisions for training and evaluation. On SearchDecision-Bench, SearchJev improves decision quality over same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models, achieves 5.2-5.3 times faster decisions, and reduces average expected calibration error by 41-74%. On BrowseComp-Plus, the dual-system agents achieve a 3.7-4.7 times speedup in active search time while improving answer accuracy from 45% to up to 54%.
item.dc:creator: Congfeng Cao, Lipeng Zuo, Konstantinos Papakostas, Qiwei Xu, Songwei Xu, Qianru Meng, Lun Zhou, Zhaochun Ren, Yougang Lyu, Xiaohui Yan

item.title: ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2610.28569v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modeling lifetime user behavior sequences is essential for capturing long-range preferences in industrial recommendation, yet sequences containing up to 100K interactions make target-aware ranking prohibitively expensive. Search-based methods that retrieve from raw sequences incur candidate-dependent costs that grow with sequence length, whereas latent compression methods reduce computation at the expense of item-level addressability. We propose ECHO (Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators), a framework that balances efficiency and fine-grained retrieval by retaining a subset of original event records per user through a Distilled Selector (DS) and retrieving a smaller set of target-relevant records for each candidate through a Target-aware Fine-grained Retriever (TFR). DS is supervised by a candidate-aware full-history teacher via per-target distillation, enabling target-aware user-level selection without requiring full-history computation for every candidate. The retriever and target-attention scorer share the relevance parameters learned by the teacher, ensuring consistent relevance estimation throughout the cascade. At a sequence length of 100K, ECHO reduces online sequence-branch FLOPs by approximately 160 times compared with a representative end-to-end model. Three deployment optimizations, including common user inputs, compact record encoding, and key-side projection absorption, further reduce memory, storage, and data-movement overhead. Experiments on KuaiRand-1K and an industrial-scale short-video platform demonstrate relative GAUC improvements ranging from 0.113% to 1.520% over state-of-the-art baselines across multiple tasks. Furthermore, online A/B tests in two production scenarios, Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite, show that ECHO improves app usage time by 0.240% and 0.373%, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Wenhao Li, Qinglin Jia, Chenghou Jin, Zihong Xian, Jiezhou Ji, Yanzhi Liu, Zezheng Wang, Bo Chen, Ruiming Tang, Chaoyi Ma, Zhaojie Liu, Wenwu Ou

item.title: FormBench: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Retrieval in Formulation Patents
item.description: arXiv:2610.30175v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce FormBench, a platform for testing the ability of models to retrieve precise chemical information from technical documents. FormBench contains 55,352 queries and two retrieval corpus variants each with ~1M passages: FormBench-Random (C0), with randomly sampled distractors, and FormBench-Structured (C1), with structurally proximate distractors. Each query is paired with an anchor passage, a hard negative, and a soft negative - derived from a materials ontology through entity overlap scoring, providing a deeper graded signal on a model's discriminatory power. We evaluate 10 model configurations spanning commercial API encoders (OpenAI, Voyage), open-source encoders (Nomic, GTE-large, Qwen3-Embed), and their task-adaptive fine-tuned (TAPT) variants. We find: (1) commercial APIs score very poorly across all configurations (OpenAI-3-large: 0.009 on C1, 0.213 on C0); (2) TAPT on FormBench triplets lifts Qwen3-Embed to 0.4085 on C1, 0.4835 on C0; (3) BM25 remains competitive (0.375 on C1, 0.467 on C0), exceeded only by TAPT-Qwen3; (4) corpus size has a significant impact on retrieval behavior, as demonstrated through a corpus-size ablation; (5) the API failure traces to within-domain geometric collapse; (6) APIs outperform even the TAPT variants on classification and clustering tasks. FormBench is released in BEIR-compatible format at huggingface.co/datasets/vinven7/FormBench under CC-BY-4.0.
item.dc:creator: Vineeth Venugopal, Elsa Olivetti, Jonathan Welch

item.title: The Delayed Countdown Method for Validating Review-Oriented AI Workflows in eDiscovery
item.description: arXiv:2610.31311v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Review-oriented workflows have become the dominant approach to AI-assisted document review in electronic discovery (eDiscovery). How to validate the effectiveness of review-oriented workflows has, however, remained a confusing and controversial topic in technology-assisted review (TAR) in the law. We examine the sources of this controversy, and propose a simple and practical evaluation approach for review-oriented workflows. Our Delayed Countdown method is easily incorporated into existing review-oriented workflows and software, is compatible with arbitrary stopping rules, and produces valid frequentist confidence intervals on effectiveness. We explain the conceptual foundations of the method, provide example computations, discuss the handling of logically impossible recall values, and suggest future work on decreasing review costs. (This paper was submitted October 1, 2026 to The Tenth Annual Workshop on Applications of Artificial Intelligence in the Legal Industry.)
item.dc:creator: David D. Lewis, Tara Emory, Lenora Gray, Mark Noel, Jeremy Pickens, Eugene Yang

item.title: Separating Thinking from Spelling for Efficient Generative Recommendation
item.description: arXiv:2610.32980v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative recommenders retrieve items by writing their semantic IDs (SIDs) code by code under trie-constrained beam search, an approach now deployed on large web platforms. Standard autoregressive interfaces pay for the SID length K twice: a history of T items enters the backbone as TK code tokens, and every beam-search step runs through the backbone, so returning B candidates costs O(BK) backbone decode tokens per user. The second cost often dominates, and it grows with the backbone, the SID depth and the candidate budget. We introduce Deco (decoding from concepts), which separates reading the history from writing the identifier. The backbone reads each history item as one fused token and condenses the history once into a compact next-item concept; a light KV-cached decoder conditioned on the concept and the generated prefix runs the entire beam search, while the identifiers, the trie and the autoregressive factorization stay unchanged. The decoder approaches full-backbone accuracy with cross-entropy alone, and distillation improves it further. On seven datasets from e-commerce, movies and music streaming, Deco achieves comparable or better accuracy than both a standard generative recommender and the full-backbone teacher with fused inputs, while delivering 3.2-8.6$\times$ their throughput under a 50 ms p95 latency budget in a production-style serving pipeline. Delegating beam search makes larger candidate pools and models practical: Deco generates 1000 candidates faster than its teacher generates 100, and with a 1.5B-parameter LLM backbone, it matches the 69M-parameter teacher's throughput while achieving higher accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Danil Gusak, Anna Volodkevich, Ivan Oseledets, Evgeny Frolov

item.title: Improving the Performance of Compressed Transformers with Post-Hoc Embedding Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2602.14635v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Model compression is necessary for deployment of transformer models in resource-constrained environments. However, compression reduces the performance of transformer models on downstream tasks. Existing solutions such as Knowledge Distillation (KD) and Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) have their own limitations. KD trains the student under the teacher's supervision, but needs the teacher's training pipeline. PEFT methods such as LoRA adapt a model to a new task, but they do not recover the loss caused by compression. Our intuition is that a compressed model can be improved by aligning its token embeddings with those of a better performing reference model. We learn this alignment with a small feed-forward Alignment Adapter (AlAd) placed after the final layer of the compressed model. AlAd reads a window of neighbouring tokens, so it can use local context. AlAd is trained post-hoc, after the compressed model has been produced. The compressed model can either be kept frozen or jointly fine-tuned with AlAd. We study the effect of AlAd with BERT-base as the reference model and four compressed variants of the BERT family. We evaluate AlAd on three token-level tasks: POS tagging, NER and Extractive Question Answering. AlAd improves performance of compressed models on all three tasks. Joint fine-tuning gives a larger improvement in performance. The performance gain is the largest for the smallest models. AlAd provides a favorable trade-off between the efficiency and the performance of compressed models.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Raj Rai, Abhishek Dhaka, Amit Awekar

item.title: Good Scores, Bad Data: A Metric for Multimodal Coherence
item.description: arXiv:2603.25924v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal AI systems are evaluated by downstream task accuracy, but high accuracy does not mean the underlying data is coherent. A model can score well on Visual Question Answering (VQA) while its inputs contradict each other. We introduce the Multimodal Coherence Score (MCS), a metric that evaluates fusion quality independent of any downstream model. MCS decomposes coherence into four dimensions, identity, spatial, semantic, and decision, with weights learned via Nelder-Mead optimization. We evaluate on 1,000 Visual Genome images using DETR, CLIP, and ViLT, and validate on 150 COCO images with no retraining. Across three fusion architectures, MCS discriminates quality with higher sensitivity than task accuracy alone (Spearman rho = 0.093 vs. 0.071). Perturbation experiments confirm each dimension responds independently to its failure mode with zero cross-talk. MCS is lightweight, requires no human annotation, and tells you not just that something broke, but what broke.
item.dc:creator: Vasundra Srinivasan

item.title: Finding Change in Satellite Archives from Text: How to Combine Before-and-After Images Efficiently
item.description: arXiv:2607.28571v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Operational Earth observation increasingly calls for answering queries such as ``find the image pairs where a new building appeared.'' This means searching an archive of before-and-after (bi-temporal) satellite image pairs and ranking each pair by how well it matches a natural-language description of the change. The component that performs this match, the fusion module that combines the ``before'' and ``after'' views, must be run at query time across many candidate pairs, so its speed largely sets the cost of every search. We present a controlled comparison of how to build that module. Using one fixed image encoder (a frozen CLIP model) and one training recipe for all variants, we evaluate eight designs drawn from three families: attention, state-space models (Mamba), and learned compression (our Temporal Bottleneck Fusion, TBF). Each design is tested on two benchmarks (LEVIR-CC and Dubai-CC) with ten random seeds, so the reported differences are statistically grounded. We outline three findings: first, a training-free two-stage search (a cheap difference model that shortlists candidates, followed by attention fusion that re-ranks them) matches or exceeds full-fusion recall on LEVIR-CC while cutting query cost $10$-$15\times$, with comparable R@1/R@5 on Dubai-CC; second, the linear-time scan of Mamba, attractive on paper, gives no speed benefit at the patch counts typical of vision transformers ($L{=}196$): the scan is limited by memory bandwidth, whereas attention maps cleanly onto parallel hardware; and third, compressing the fused representation (TBF) reduces parameters by $2.3\times$ and latency by $1.6\times$ for a change-only BLEU-1 cost of $0.007$, although more aggressive compression quietly discards change-relevant detail that aggregate metrics fail to reveal.
item.dc:creator: Simon Roy, Mark Bong, Giovanni Beltrame

item.title: CoinRAG: Contextualized Information Nugget KV Cache Reuse for Long-Context RAG
item.description: arXiv:2608.07458v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent optimization studies on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) have exploited chunk-level KV cache reuse to avoid processing long retrieved contexts for higher efficiency, while significant information redundancy and noise still remain in the coarse-grained chunks. This paper optimizes the Pareto frontier under low prefill latency constraints while maximizing accuracy by proposing CoinRAG (Contextualized Information Nugget KV Cache Reuse for Long-Context RAG). The name metaphorically reflects our core mechanism: much like assembling small tokens (or "coins") to accumulate a larger value, CoinRAG compositionally reuses offline-computed, fine-grained nugget caches to form a learned contextual representation efficiently in a more semantically relevant but compact manner. Specifically, instead of full-chunk encoding, CoinRAG identifies query-relevant semantic units within retrieved chunks through two-stage retrieval and seamlessly assembles their sliced KV representations with a chunk-level context. CoinRAG can be integrated with CacheBlend's selective recomputation for further accuracy gains under the same latency budget. Extensive evaluations on LongBench multi-hop question answering tasks demonstrate that CoinRAG substantially shortens the active context and outperforms the other baselines with a new Pareto frontier and an average 5.3% relative improvement in answer quality (F1) under a standard fast prefill latency budget.
item.dc:creator: Gyuwan Kim, Cheoneum Park, Tao Yang

item.title: 5W1H+Which: Context-Valid Semantic Indexing with Progressive Ontology Binding
item.description: arXiv:2609.35184v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Semantic indexing must preserve reusable source information without committing too early to one business schema, while providing checkable premises for reasoning. We propose 5W1H+Which, a design that separates source-grounded content extraction from progressive ontology binding. The 5W1H questions organize independently addressable content units; Which records links to versioned ontology elements, mapping relations, applicability scopes, and validation states. Time, location, system environment, and participant roles constrain when facts, bindings, and rules may be used. Unbound content remains searchable, whereas formal reasoning requires explicit premise checks. The design distinguishes business valid time, system knowledge time, and operational traces, and tracks dependencies for revalidation and incremental maintenance. Worked examples illustrate cloud migration and temporal policy validity. The resulting linked corpus can support downstream training and evaluation organized around benchmarks, positive and negative examples, trajectories, and costs. Trajectories preserve steps, evidence-backed checkpoints, recovery, and local-to-global failure impact; reusable skills remain downstream abstractions requiring cross-episode validation. We specify falsifiable hypotheses and capability-matched baselines to test cross-task evidence coverage, contextual misuse, and update cost under equal information and budgets. The contribution is a proposed indexing and maintenance contract, not a new universal ontology or post-training algorithm. No experiments have yet been conducted, and no performance improvement is claimed.
item.dc:creator: Yaxiao Liu (PwC China AI Center), Pengbo Liu (PwC China AI Center), Yiwen Liu (PwC China AI Center), Yihua Guan (PwC China AI Center), Jiaxing Song (Tsinghua University)

item.title: Comparing GenAI to Machine Learning and Manual Review for eDiscovery
item.description: arXiv:2610.16925v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Keeling et al. [Keeling2026Generative] report on a case study recently conducted by Redgrave LLP in which they assert that Relativity's Generative AI Review tool (aiR) achieved 88% recall while Relativity Assisted Learning (RAL), its machine-learning tool, achieved 64% recall. These results are not comparable because the methods employed have different objectives, because of inter-assessor disagreement, and because they represent different recall-precision and cost-benefit trade-offs. Our analysis of the Redgrave data indicates that, when these differences are taken into account, aiR and manual review are comparable. Furthermore, established machine-learning models employing Continuous Active Learning (CAL) and Scalable Continuous Active Learning (S-CAL) show state-of-the-art effectiveness, and superior efficiency, when trained only on a sample of 2,000 first-pass-reviewer responsiveness determinations.
item.dc:creator: Gordon V. Cormack, Maura R. Grossman

item.title: The Geometry of Agent Memory: Forecasting Retrieval-Bound Memory Failures, and Characterizing Its Limits
item.description: arXiv:2610.26433v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study whether geometric relationships between conversation turns, memory texts, and queries can predict answer correctness before generation. We evaluate four memory implementations with dense or hybrid retrieval and one observation-summary comparator. We embed these texts in a shared space. A logistic classifier uses 25 features describing query proximity, memory-conversation correspondence, and conversation structure. On LongMemEval-small, pooled AUROC is 0.640 over 2,367 question-system pairs, below a question-difficulty baseline of 0.655. Performance varies by question type: geometry reaches 0.841 on single-session-assistant questions, but system identity alone reaches 0.826. After controlling for difficulty and identity, geometry adds no statistically established pooled improvement (delta = +0.002, 95% CI [-0.010, 0.014]). A fixed-store context-selection experiment finds higher accuracy with proximity-ranked memories than with random subsets, consistent with ordinary retrieval relevance. On LoCoMo, nearest-turn similarity has modest predictive value for single-hop questions and near-chance estimates for several other categories. Training uses correctness labels; prediction uses pre-answer features and no additional LLM generation call. The results characterize associations between memory representations and correctness, rather than establish a reliable deployment diagnostic. In particular, embedding proximity does not verify fact coverage or distinguish memory-construction, retrieval, and generation errors.

item.title: Beyond Behavioral Accuracy: Evaluating Individual-Level Fidelity in LLM Investor Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.26524v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as user simulators, but can they faithfully reproduce an individual's behavior and decision logic over time? We investigate this question in a longitudinal paper-trading study with 80 participants. Using rolling next-day predictions, we evaluate trading activity, buy-sell structure, asset selection, and portfolio outcomes, complemented by controlled input ablations and participant-rated explanation alignment. No evaluated LLM reliably outperforms a simple recent-activity persistence baseline for predicting trade occurrence, while buy-sell structure and asset selection remain difficult to reproduce. Similar activity-level performance can also yield substantially different portfolio trajectories. Ablations show that activity predictions depend primarily on recent trades, whereas asset choices are sensitive to multiple evidence sources. Participants rate explanations as more aligned with their recurring strategies than with their decision-specific rationales. These findings reveal a gap between coarse behavioral agreement and individual-level fidelity, motivating separate evaluation of behavioral accuracy, explanation alignment, and evidence dependence in personalized user simulation.
item.dc:creator: Jiajie He, Yuanhong Jiang, Xintong Chen, Dongling Ni, Wenjin Liu

item.title: Scriptorium: System Design and Implementation of a Multi-Human, Multi-AI Collaborative Digital Library Search Platform
item.description: arXiv:2610.28929v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This technical report documents the design and implementation of Scriptorium, a digital library search interface designed to support multi-human, multi-AI collaboration: full cross-user transparency of search activity combined with a Manager--Worker architecture of seven role-specialized generative AI agents. A companion short demonstration paper describes Scriptorium's interaction design; because a demonstration format is constrained to a few pages, it necessarily omits most implementation detail. This report documents Scriptorium's complete system architecture, data model, collaborative-interaction design rationale, and AI orchestration mechanism, including verbatim agent prompts, the deterministic guardrails that constrain them, the language model and retrieval configuration, and the steps needed to run the system, so that the design can be inspected, critiqued, reproduced, and reused by other researchers. We also discuss the system's current limitations and the user study we are planning to evaluate its central hypothesis: that combining collaborative transparency with scoped multi-agent AI assistance increases serendipitous cross-pollination between collaborators' research threads.
